You might think this means if you plant 1 unit of GM seed and 1 unit of natural seed that the GM seed would end up producing let's say 1.2 as much product as the natural seed. This isn't true. What GM offers is easier pesticide/herbicide treatment. In areas where farming technology is dated this can provide substantial gains in yield. In the modern developed world, these gains are nullified by technology. There was a study that looked at the yield of GM crop in the US compared against natural crop in Western Europe. The natural crops actually had slightly higher yield.

The study GM advocates generally reference to show yield increase (and pesticide decrease) is this. It's a meta-analysis which means they take lots of data and combine it all together. In this case they included lots of cases where Monsanto went into undeveloped countries, provided GM crop and complete pesticide/herbicide/etc treatment. These show large gains. But in developed areas the change is effectively 0. You can see this in that paper's own graphs. The large chunk of gains are around 0 and then it's brought way up by the studies done in very undeveloped areas. The herbicide and pesticide treatments are what increases the yield, but the GM seed gets all the credit. Further confounding this data is the fact that most of these studies were published with GM funding at some point. They are under no obligation to publish results that don't support their narrative.
